scenes.say: Four documents tell the whole financial story of a business. Learn what each one answers and you can read any company's accounts.

scenes.heading: The four statements
scenes.say: The four financial statements are the income statement, the statement of owner's equity, the balance sheet, and the statement of cash flows.

scenes.heading: The question each answers
items: Income statement: did we make a profit?
Owner's equity: how did the owner's stake change?
Balance sheet: what do we own and owe?
Cash flows: where did the cash go?
scenes.say: Each answers one question. The income statement shows whether the business made a profit over a period. The statement of owner's equity shows how the owner's stake changed. The balance sheet shows what the business owns and owes on one date. And the statement of cash flows shows where cash came from and where it went.

sub: Income statement: 'for the month ended June 30'
Balance sheet: 'as of June 30'
scenes.say: Watch the headings. The income statement covers a period of time, for the month ended June thirtieth. The balance sheet is a snapshot at a single point, as of June thirtieth.

scenes.heading: Redwood River Supply · June
scenes.note: Income statement for the month ended June 30
scenes.say: Here's Redwood River Supply's first month. Service revenue of nine thousand dollars, less expenses of six thousand five hundred, gives net income of two thousand five hundred. You'll see that number again in the next statement.

scenes.q: Which statement shows what the business owns and owes on a single date?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which statement shows what a business owns and owes on a single date? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, the balance sheet. A snapshot, not a period.

scenes.say: Every balance sheet is built from just three ingredients. Here they are.

sub: Resources the business owns or controls
that will bring future benefit
scenes.say: Assets are resources the business owns or controls that it expects to bring future benefit. Cash, money customers owe you, inventory, equipment, buildings, land.

sub: What the business owes to others
scenes.say: Liabilities are what the business owes to outsiders. Money owed to suppliers, called accounts payable, wages owed to staff, and bank loans.

sub: The owner's claim on the assets:
what is left after liabilities
scenes.say: Owner's equity is the owner's claim on the assets, the part left after every liability is paid. It goes up when the owner invests or the business earns a profit, and down when the owner withdraws money or the business makes a loss.

scenes.heading: Current or noncurrent?
items: Current: used or due within one year
Equipment, buildings, long-term loans are not
scenes.say: Assets and liabilities are split into current and noncurrent. Current means they'll be used up, turned into cash, or paid within one year. Cash, receivables and supplies are current. Equipment, buildings and a five-year bank loan are noncurrent.

scenes.q: Redwood River Supply owes its supplier $1,200. What is this?
scenes.say: Quick check. Redwood River Supply owes its supplier twelve hundred dollars. What is that? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, a liability. Specifically, accounts payable.

scenes.say: Profit has two ingredients going up and two going down. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in this course.

sub: Earned from the main business activity
scenes.say: Revenue is what a business earns from its main activity, selling goods or providing services. For Redwood River Supply, repair and delivery fees are revenue.

sub: Costs used up to earn revenue
scenes.say: Expenses are the costs used up in earning that revenue: wages, rent, utilities, fuel, advertising.

scenes.heading: Gains and losses
items: Come from side events, not the main business
Gain: sell old equipment for more than book value
Loss: sell it for less, or a theft or flood
scenes.say: Gains and losses come from events outside the main business. If Redwood River sells an old truck for more than its value in the books, that's a gain. If it sells for less, or is stolen, that's a loss.

scenes.heading: Putting it together
scenes.say: On the income statement, revenue and gains increase net income, and expenses and losses reduce it. Nine thousand, less six thousand five hundred, plus a four hundred dollar gain, gives net income of two thousand nine hundred.

scenes.q: Redwood River pays $800 rent for its workshop. What is this?
scenes.say: Quick check. Redwood River pays eight hundred dollars rent for its workshop. What is it? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, an expense. Rent is a normal cost of running the business.

scenes.say: The four statements aren't separate documents. They're one chain, and a number flows from each into the next.

scenes.heading: Prepare them in this order
scenes.say: That's why we prepare them in order. First the income statement, then the statement of owner's equity, then the balance sheet, and finally the statement of cash flows.

scenes.heading: Statement of owner's equity
scenes.say: Dana started with nothing, invested twenty thousand dollars, and the business earned two thousand five hundred from the income statement. She withdrew one thousand for personal use. So ending capital is twenty-one thousand five hundred.

sub: Ending capital is the equity line
on the June 30 balance sheet
scenes.say: That ending capital, twenty-one thousand five hundred, becomes the owner's equity figure on the June thirtieth balance sheet.

sub: Balance sheet cash = ending cash
on the statement of cash flows
scenes.say: And the cash shown on the balance sheet equals the ending cash on the statement of cash flows. Change one number in the chain and the others must change too.

scenes.q: Net income flows first into which statement?
scenes.say: Quick check. Net income flows first into which statement? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, the statement of owner's equity, and from there into the balance sheet.

scenes.say: Redwood River fixes a tractor in June but gets paid in July. Which month gets the revenue? Your answer depends on the basis of accounting.

sub: Record revenue when cash is received
and expenses when cash is paid
scenes.say: Under the cash basis, revenue is recorded when cash comes in and expenses when cash goes out. It's simple, and some small businesses use it for tax.

sub: Record revenue when earned
and expenses when incurred
scenes.say: Under the accrual basis, revenue is recorded when it's earned and expenses when they're incurred, whatever happens to the cash. GAAP requires the accrual basis.

scenes.heading: The tractor repair
scenes.say: So the tractor repair goes in July under the cash basis, when the money arrives, but in June under the accrual basis, because that's when the work was done.

scenes.heading: Two principles behind accrual
items: Expense recognition: match costs to the revenue they helped earn
scenes.say: Two principles drive this. The revenue recognition principle says record revenue when it's earned. The expense recognition principle, often called matching, says record expenses in the same period as the revenue they helped produce.

scenes.q: Under the accrual basis, when is revenue recorded?
scenes.say: Quick check. Under the accrual basis, when is revenue recorded? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, when it's earned. Cash timing doesn't decide it.

scenes.say: A bank looks at your balance sheet with one question: can this business pay what it owes in the next twelve months? A classified balance sheet makes that easy to see.

sub: Groups assets and liabilities
into current and noncurrent
scenes.say: A classified balance sheet groups assets and liabilities into current and noncurrent sections, so the short-term picture stands out.

scenes.heading: Redwood River Supply · June 30
scenes.say: Here's Redwood River at June thirtieth. Fourteen thousand of current assets and eighteen thousand noncurrent, thirty-two thousand in total. On the other side, seven thousand current liabilities, three and a half thousand noncurrent, and owner's equity of twenty-one five. That's thirty-two thousand again. It balances.

sub: Current assets − current liabilities
scenes.say: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. Fourteen thousand minus seven thousand gives seven thousand dollars of cushion.

sub: Current assets ÷ current liabilities
Two dollars of current assets per dollar owed
scenes.say: The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities. Fourteen thousand over seven thousand is two point zero. Redwood River has two dollars of current assets for every dollar it owes in the next year.

scenes.q: Current assets $9,000, current liabilities $6,000. Current ratio?
scenes.say: Quick check. Current assets nine thousand, current liabilities six thousand. What's the current ratio? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, one point five. Nine thousand divided by six thousand. Three thousand would be the working capital.
